tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

## Hauling Stone and Timber: The Origins of the Wagonway

The railway is a surface built to carry a load along a path that does not wander. Its history begins with the simple observation that a wheel rolling along a smooth, fixed track meets less resistance than a wheel grinding through mud or ruts. Long before anyone put a boiler on wheels, people had learned to lay paved or grooved ways to ease the movement of heavy things, and the railway is best understood as the last and most consequential step in that long line of improvements.

The most famous early example is the Diolkos, a paved trackway that crossed the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece. Built around the sixth century BC, it carried ships, or more probably their cargoes and small vessels on wheeled wooden cradles, across the narrow land bridge so that they could avoid the dangerous sea passage around the Peloponnese. Ancient sources describe the way as a stone-paved road with grooves cut into it to guide the wheels. Whether the Diolkos was truly a rail in the modern sense is debatable, since its function was closer to a portage than to a line of transport in the later sense, but it demonstrates that the principle of guiding wheels along a prepared surface was understood very early.

Medieval and early modern Europe provided the more direct ancestors. In the mines of central Europe, from at least the fifteenth century, workers pushed carts loaded with ore along timber planks. The planks reduced friction and kept the cart from sinking into soft ground. The German mining writer Georgius Agricola, in his great treatise *De re metallica*, published in 1556, illustrated the carts and the wooden trackways used to move ore out of shafts and tunnels. These early wooden ways were laid as simple lines of timber, and they were usually worked by human or animal power. The wheels were often flanged or the rails were fitted with a guide on one side, so the cart did not slide off. Mining, with its heavy loads, difficult terrain, and need for a steady supply of raw material, was the environment in which these ideas were first refined.

The English coal trade moved this technology to a much larger scale. By the late seventeenth century, the coalfields of the River Tyne in northeast England were sending large quantities of coal to London and the coast. Coal had to be brought from pit heads, often several miles inland, to the riverside staithes where it could be loaded into collier ships. Horses hauled wagons along wooden rails, and these wagonways became a familiar feature of the landscape around Newcastle, Sunderland, and the Wear valley. The wooden rails wore quickly, and the early wagonways used a variety of solutions. In some cases the rails were capped with a strip of iron to extend their life. The flanged wheel, which ran on the inside of the rail, is commonly associated with these early systems, while the flangeless wheel that ran on a rail with its own guide flange came later.

The metal rail was the next development. In 1767, at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire, the ironmasters of the Darby family and their associates were producing cast iron in quantity, and iron rails began to replace timber. Cast iron was brittle, and early iron rails were prone to fracture under heavy loads, but they lasted far longer than wood and could be produced in standard shapes. The so-called plateway, in which the wheel had a flange and ran on a flat iron plate with a raised edge, was widely used in the late eighteenth century. The edge rail, in which the wheel ran on top of a rail and had a flange of its own, was pioneered in the same period by engineers such as Josias Jessop on routes including the Cromford and High Peak Railway. The edge rail eventually prevailed because it allowed a smoother, more efficient wheel, and it became the basis of the standard railway track that exists today.

By the end of the eighteenth century, then, Britain had a substantial network of horse-drawn wagonways. These lines were mostly private, serving particular collieries, ironworks, or quarries. They were not public carriers in the sense that a canal or turnpike road was public, and they were built for the convenience of a single owner. Yet they carried a remarkable volume of freight, and they taught a generation of engineers how to lay out a track, how to grade it, how to build bridges and embankments for it, and how to manage the wear and the maintenance it required. The wagonway was a school of railway engineering long before the locomotive appeared.

## The Steam Locomotive Arrives

The steam engine had its own separate history. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, introduced in 1712, used steam and then cold water to create a partial vacuum in a cylinder, so that atmospheric pressure drove a piston down. These engines were inefficient, consuming large quantities of fuel, but they were robust and they found a use pumping water out of mines. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769, and his later improvements to the rotary engine and the double-acting cylinder, made steam power far more economical and versatile. By the 1780s, Watt's engines were being used in factories and mills across Britain, and the notion of a steam engine that could drive machinery by rotary motion had become familiar.

The leap from stationary engine to mobile locomotive took most of the following generation. Engineers in Cornwall, the centre of the mining engine trade, were among the first to experiment with steam for transport. Richard Trevithick, a Cornish engineer whose high-pressure steam engines were smaller and lighter than Watt's, built a road carriage in 1801, and he followed it with a locomotive designed for the rails. On 21 February 1804, at the Penydarren ironworks in South Wales, Trevithick's locomotive hauled a load of iron and seventy men along a tramroad to the Merthyr Tydfil area. The journey covered about nine and three-quarter miles and took several hours. It is generally regarded as the first journey by a steam locomotive on rails, though the engine was too heavy for the cast iron rails of the time and broke several of them. Trevithick did not pursue the idea commercially, and his locomotives were not put into regular service.

The problem was adhesion. A smooth wheel on a smooth rail might not grip enough to pull a heavy train, and the weight of early locomotives was a serious concern for the cast iron track beneath them. Several solutions were tried. Matthew Murray, of Leeds, built locomotives in 1811 for the Middleton Railway, which ran from the colliery at Middleton to Leeds. John Blenkinsop, the Middleton Railway's manager, patented a system in which the locomotive drove a toothed wheel that engaged with a toothed rack laid along one rail. The rack provided grip, and the engines could haul heavier loads than the friction of a smooth wheel would allow. The Middleton locomotives, the first to enter regular commercial service, ran on this rack-and-pinion principle from 1812, and they can be considered the first successful commercial steam railway.

Other engineers soon found simpler answers. William Hedley's locomotive Puffing Billy, built for the Wylam colliery near Newcastle around 1813, is one of the oldest surviving steam locomotives in the world, now preserved in the Science Museum in London. Hedley's engine ran on smooth wheels, which proved that adhesion alone could serve for moderate loads if the engine was light enough to avoid breaking the rails. Timothy Hackworth, who worked with Hedley and later built locomotives for the Stockton and Darlington Railway, also contributed to the design. Hackworth's work with blast pipes, which used the exhaust steam to draw the fire and increase steaming power, was one of the decisive technical improvements of the period.

George Stephenson, a self-taught engineer who had risen from a fireman at a colliery to become a respected mechanical engineer, was the most significant of these builders. At Killingworth, near Newcastle, he built the locomotive Blücher in 1814, one of the first to run successfully on smooth wheels and to haul coal along the colliery's wagonway. Stephenson's engines improved steadily. He added the multitubular boiler, which increased the heating surface and the power of the engine, and he worked with his son Robert, who would later become the leading locomotive builder in Britain. The locomotive that emerged from this development was no longer a curiosity. It was a machine capable of pulling heavy loads on a dependable basis, and by the 1820s the case for using it on public railways had become strong.

## The First Public Railways

The Stockton and Darlington Railway, authorised by Parliament in 1821 and opened in 1825, is generally regarded as the first public railway to carry passengers and freight using steam locomotives. It was conceived as a coal carrier, linking collieries in the Durham coalfield with the port at Stockton and the Tees, but its promoters also anticipated that it would be open to other users. Stephenson was engaged as engineer and built the locomotive Locomotion No. 1, which hauled the opening train on 27 September 1825. The railway's passenger services were initially run by horses as well as locomotives, and the mixture of motive power reflected the uncertainty of the period. Yet the S&DR demonstrated that a railway could serve a community and turn a profit, and it set the template for the rail companies that followed.

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was the project that proved the steam railway could compete with the best of the older transport systems. Liverpool was the port through which Britain's cotton trade passed, and Manchester was its manufacturing centre. The canal between them was crowded and slow, and the two cities were keen to link themselves more efficiently. The railway was promoted in the 1820s, with George Stephenson as engineer, and it faced fierce opposition from landowners, canal interests, and the owners of turnpike roads. The line was authorised in 1826 and construction was difficult, requiring the crossing of Chat Moss, a boggy peat bog that had to be floated on bundles of brushwood and earth, and the cutting of substantial rock sections.

The question of what kind of locomotive should haul the line's trains was settled by the Rainhill Trials, held in October 1829. The directors of the railway offered a prize of £500 for a locomotive that could meet specified performance criteria, including hauling a load of several times its own weight at a minimum average speed. Several entrants came forward, among them Timothy Hackworth's Sans Pareil, the Novelty of John Braithwaite and John Ericsson, and Stephenson's Rocket, built with the assistance of his son Robert. The Rocket was the only entry to meet all the conditions, and it did so with a design that incorporated the multitubular boiler, a blast pipe, and a horizontal cylinder arrangement that would become the model for many later locomotives. Its speed on the trials reached around thirty miles per hour, which was remarkable for the time, and its reliability convinced the directors that steam locomotion was practical.

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. The opening was marred by tragedy. William Huskisson, the Member of Parliament for Liverpool and a senior government figure, had been present at the ceremony, and during a stop at Parkside he stepped out onto the track to greet the Duke of Wellington. He was struck by the Rocket, which was moving on the adjacent line, and he died of his injuries. The accident was widely reported and it shocked the public, yet it did little to dampen enthusiasm for the railway. The line was a commercial success from its first years, carrying cotton, passengers, and goods at speeds and costs that its rivals could not match. Within a decade, the railway had shown that steam transport could be safe enough, fast enough, and economical enough to be a serious competitor to every other form of inland carriage.

## The Railway Age in Britain

The years following the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway saw the creation of a national network. The Railway Mania of the 1840s was the most dramatic phase of this expansion. Investors in Britain, flush with capital from the industrial boom and attracted by the returns that the early railways had shown, subscribed enormous sums to new projects. Parliament received hundreds of bills proposing new lines, and many of them were promoted by speculators who had little interest in building railways but a great deal of interest in selling shares. The bubble burst in 1845 and 1846, and many companies failed, leaving investors with heavy losses and a legacy of unfinished or unnecessary lines. Yet the mania also built a large part of the network that Britain would use for the next century. By the late 1840s, the main trunk routes connecting London to the major cities of England, Scotland, and Wales had been either completed or authorised.

The rivalry between two gauges became one of the most publicised disputes of the period. The gauge is the distance between the inner faces of the two rails, and the standard gauge of 4 feet 8½ inches derived from the wagonways of the north-east of England, where the first locomotives had been built to suit existing tramroad dimensions. Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the engineer of the Great Western Railway, chose a broader gauge of 7 feet ¼ inch for his line from London to Bristol and beyond. Brunel argued that a wider gauge would offer greater stability, higher speeds, and more room for the boiler and machinery of the locomotive. Supporters of the standard gauge argued that the existing network was already built to that gauge, and that a break of gauge would make through running impossible. The dispute was settled in favour of the standard gauge by a parliamentary commission and by the Gauge Act of 1846, which required new lines to use the standard gauge except in certain specified cases. The broad gauge survived for a time on the Great Western, but it was gradually converted to standard gauge in the 1890s, and the last broad gauge line was closed in 1892.

The Great Western Railway itself deserves particular mention. Brunel designed a route that ran as directly as the terrain allowed, using gentle gradients and long straight sections, and he built some of the most ambitious bridges and viaducts of the century. The Royal Albert Bridge at Saltash, across the Tamar, was completed in 1859, and it carried the railway into Cornwall on a series of iron tubes supported by a graceful arch. Brunel also built the Clifton Suspension Bridge, though that structure was not completed during his lifetime and was finished by others. The Great Western's trains were among the fastest in the world at the time, and the company's express services between London and Bristol established a reputation for speed and comfort that the rest of the network would strive to match.

The other great railway companies of the period also left their mark on the landscape. The London and North Western Railway became one of the largest companies in the world, with a network that linked London with the industrial north and with Scotland. The Midland Railway built a route from London to Leeds and Bradford and developed a substantial freight business. The North Eastern Railway served the coalfields and the industrial towns of Yorkshire and the north-east. By the end of the nineteenth century, the railway companies of Britain had built a network of some twenty thousand miles of track, and they had created a dense system of stations, goods yards, engine sheds, and signal boxes. The railway had become a central part of British life, carrying passengers to work, transporting goods to market, and bringing holidaymakers to the seaside.

The question of regulation was never far from the surface. The early railways were promoted by private companies under acts of Parliament, and their fares and services were subject to only limited control. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844, often called the Gladstone Act after its sponsor, required companies to provide a basic third-class passenger service at a low fare, and it gave the state the right to purchase railways after a set period. Later acts increased the power of the Board of Trade to inspect and approve new lines. The accidents that the railways produced, particularly the collisions and derailments that occurred as traffic grew, led to steady improvements in safety. The Regulation of Railways Act of 1889 gave the Board of Trade stronger powers in response to a series of serious accidents, including the Armagh disaster of 1889, and it required the adoption of safety measures such as the continuous brake.

## Railways Across Europe and the Americas

The railway spread rapidly beyond Britain. Belgium, which had gained independence in 1830 and was keen to develop its economy, built the first railway on the continent to carry passengers under a national plan. The line between Brussels and Mechelen opened in 1835, and the Belgian state built a network that linked the major cities and the ports. The Belgian railway was an early model for state involvement in railway construction, and the country became a centre of railway engineering and manufacturing that exported locomotives and rolling stock across Europe.

Germany's railways began with the Ludwigsbahn, a line between Nuremberg and Fürth opened in 1835. The German states were divided and each developed its own network, which made the country's railway history complicated. Prussia built its first major lines in the 1840s and later consolidated its network, and the Berlin to Potsdam line and others laid the foundation for a national system after unification in 1871. Germany became one of the great railway nations of the nineteenth century. Its locomotive builders, including Borsig in Berlin and Henschel in Kassel, produced engines for domestic and foreign railways, and the German railway administrations developed standards for safety, timetabling, and management that were widely admired.

France was slower to build a national network, in part because of the political instability of the early nineteenth century and in part because of a debate about the role of the state. The first major French railway ran between Saint-Étienne and Lyon, a line that combined horse-drawn and locomotive operation and was opened in stages in the 1820s and early 1830s. The Paris to Saint-Germain line, opened in 1837, was one of the first passenger routes in the French capital. The French state adopted a plan in 1842 that established a radial network centred on Paris, with lines to the main regions of the country, and the subsequent development of the French railway system followed this pattern. Despite the early delays, France built an extensive network and developed a distinctive engineering tradition that would later produce the high-speed trains of the late twentieth century.

Austria and the Habsburg lands had their own railway history. The Kaiser Ferdinands-Nordbahn, a railway from Vienna towards Brno and Bohemia, opened in 1837, and the empire went on to build lines across its territories, including the Semmering Pass, where the engineering challenge of crossing the Alps led to innovations in gradient, curve, and bridge design. The Semmering line, completed in 1854, is one of the classic landmarks of early railway engineering, and it remains in service today as a World Heritage site. Russia's first line, from St Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo, opened in 1837. The Russian government later built a major line from Moscow to St Petersburg in the 1840s, and the country's railway network expanded across the vast distances of the empire over the next half century. The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and completed in 1916, was the most ambitious of these projects, and it linked European Russia with the Pacific coast.

In the United States, railways developed in a different context. The country was large, its population was spread out, and there was no established network of canals or turnpikes to rival the rail lines in the way that existed in Britain. The first American railway to use steam locomotives was the Baltimore and Ohio, which began operation in 1830. Its early locomotives were imported from Britain, and the company experimented with a range of designs before settling on American-built engines. Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb, built in 1830, was a small experimental locomotive that demonstrated that steam power could work on American tracks, though its famous race against a horse, in which the locomotive's belt slipped and the horse won, is a useful reminder of the early uncertainty of the technology.

American railways developed their own track and equipment. Many early lines used strap rail, a flat iron bar fastened to a wooden stringer, which tended to curl up and pierce the floor of passenger cars, creating a hazard. The T-rail, with its wide head and vertical web, was adopted in the 1840s and became the standard form for American track. American railways also favoured the American-style locomotive, with a cow-catcher on the front, a tall smokestack, and a relatively simple frame. The gauge varied considerably across the United States in the early years, and the process of standardisation took decades, with the final gauge of 4 feet 8½ inches adopted across much of the country by the 1880s.

The most famous American railway project was the transcontinental line that linked the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento and the Union Pacific built west from Omaha, and the two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah on 10 May 1869. The golden spike ceremony marked the completion of the first continuous railway across North America. The project was financed by government land grants and loans, and it involved the labour of thousands of workers, many of them Chinese immigrants who worked on the Central Pacific and Irish immigrants who laid track on the Union Pacific. The transcontinental railway dramatically reduced the time needed to cross the continent, cutting a journey of months by wagon or ship to a matter of days. Other transcontinental lines followed, including the Northern Pacific, the Great Northern, the Santa Fe, and the Canadian Pacific, which completed its line across Canada in 1885.

Latin America and other regions also built railways, often with British, French, or American capital and engineering. Railways were built to serve mines, plantations, and ports, and the lines often reflected the export-oriented economies of the countries in which they were built. In India, the first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 between Bori Bunder in Bombay and Thane, and the country's railway network expanded rapidly under British administration. By the early twentieth century, India had one of the largest railway systems in the world, and the railway had become a vital instrument of trade, administration, and military logistics. In Africa, Australia, and elsewhere, railways were built to link interior regions to coastal ports, and their construction shaped the economic and political geography of those continents.

## Engineering, Safety, and the Control of Movement

The railway was not only a matter of locomotives and track. It required new forms of engineering to cross difficult terrain, carry heavy loads over rivers, and pass through mountains. The early railway engineers built embankments and cuttings to keep the line level, and they developed methods for laying track on soft ground and for maintaining the rails under constant use. Bridges were a central concern. Iron bridges, first used for road crossings in the eighteenth century, were adapted for railways, and engineers such as Robert Stephenson designed large structures that set the standard for the period. Stephenson's Britannia Bridge, completed in 1850, carried the railway across the Menai Strait on two massive tubular iron spans. The tubular girder was a bold experiment in structural design, and it remains a landmark of Victorian engineering.

Tunnels presented a different set of problems. The Woodhead Tunnel in England, completed in 1845, and the Box Tunnel near Bath, completed in 1841, were among the first long railway tunnels in Britain, and they required the use of ventilation and careful engineering to avoid collapse and smoke problems. The great continental tunnels followed later. The Mont Cenis, or Fréjus, tunnel between France and Italy was begun in 1857 and completed in 1871, and it used pneumatic drills powered by compressed air, an early use of mechanical rock drilling in a long tunnel. The Gotthard Tunnel in Switzerland, completed in 1882, was a further step forward, and it was followed by the Simplon Tunnel, opened in 1906, which at around twelve miles was the longest tunnel in the world at the time. These tunnels reshaped the connections between countries and made the Alps a route for international trade and travel.

Safety was a continuing concern. The early railways experienced collisions, derailments, boiler explosions, and accidents at level crossings, and the pressure to keep trains on schedule sometimes led to dangerous practices. The development of the block system, in which the line was divided into sections and only one train was allowed in each section at a time, was one of the most important safety advances. Early block working relied on telegraph communication between signal boxes, and the electric telegraph, pioneered by William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone in Britain, made the system practical. Signals, originally operated by hand, were developed into mechanical systems with interlocking, so that a signalman could not set a conflicting route. The interlocking frame, first widely used in the 1850s and 1860s, is one of the most significant safety devices in railway history, and its descendants are still in use.

The braking and coupling of trains posed their own problems. Early freight trains were braked by hand, with brakemen moving from car to car to apply the brake, and the work was dangerous and slow. Coupling was done by hand, with men standing between cars to link them with a pin and link, and this exposed workers to serious injury or death. George Westinghouse, an American engineer, developed the air brake in the late 1860s, using compressed air to apply brakes on every car of a train from the locomotive. The Westinghouse brake was adopted widely in the United States and later in Britain and elsewhere, and it greatly improved the safety and control of trains. The automatic coupler, invented by Eli Janney in the 1870s, replaced the link and pin with a device that coupled cars automatically when they were pushed together, and it too greatly reduced the number of injuries to railway workers. The federal government in the United States eventually required both devices on freight cars, and the improvements they brought were among the most important steps in making rail travel safe.

Passenger comfort also improved. Early railway carriages were little more than stagecoach bodies placed on rails, with open seating and poor suspension. The development of the bogie, a pivoting frame carrying two or more axles, allowed carriages and locomotives to take curves more smoothly. The sleeping car, pioneered by George Pullman in the United States in the 1860s, allowed long-distance travellers to rest overnight, and the dining car followed. The corridor carriage, which allowed passengers to move from one compartment to another, made long journeys more practical. Heating, lighting, and ventilation were gradually improved, and by the early twentieth century the best trains offered a level of comfort that had been unthinkable in the early years.

## Steam at Its Height and the Turn to Other Power

The steam locomotive reached its fullest development in the first half of the twentieth century. Engineers in many countries designed large, powerful engines capable of hauling heavy freight and fast passenger trains. The Pacific-type locomotive, with a four-wheel leading truck, six driving wheels, and a two-wheel trailing truck, became a standard design for express passenger service in the United States and Europe. The American Union Pacific's Big Boy, built in the early 1940s, was one of the largest steam locomotives ever constructed, and its articulated frame allowed it to haul heavy freight over the mountain grades of the western United States. The Chinese, Indian, South African, and Australian railways also built and operated large steam fleets, and steam remained the principal motive power for much of the world's railway traffic until the middle of the twentieth century.

The speed of steam locomotives reached its peak in Britain in the 1930s. On 3 July 1938, the LNER locomotive Mallard, designed by Nigel Gresley, set a world speed record for steam traction of 126 miles per hour on a descent near Stoke Bank in Lincolnshire. The record has never been beaten by a steam locomotive, and it stands as a reminder of the technical maturity that steam had reached. Mallard's streamlined casing, which was part of a wider fashion for streamlined trains in the interwar period, reflected the aerodynamic thinking of the time. The streamlined locomotives and trains of the 1930s, including the German Flying Hamburger, the American streamliners of the Pennsylvania and New York Central, and the British Coronation class, showed that railway design could be both functional and aesthetically striking.

Steam, however, had significant drawbacks. Steam locomotives were inefficient in their conversion of fuel into work, they required large amounts of coal and water, and they needed extensive servicing at engine sheds and depots. They produced smoke and cinders, and their operation was labour-intensive. The fireman, the locomotive crew member who shovelled coal into the firebox, worked in hot and dirty conditions, and the locomotive driver had to manage a complicated machine. As the twentieth century progressed, railways increasingly looked for alternatives that would reduce costs and improve reliability.

Electrification was one such alternative. The first electric railway in the modern sense was demonstrated by Werner von Siemens at the Berlin Industrial Exhibition of 1879, where a small electric locomotive hauled a train of cars on a short circular track. Electric tramways followed in the 1880s and 1890s, and Frank Sprague's work in Richmond, Virginia, in 1888, which produced a practical electric street railway, did much to establish the technology in the United States. Full-scale electric main-line railways came later. The Baltimore and Ohio's Howard Street tunnel was electrified in the 1890s, and the Liverpool Overhead Railway, opened in 1893, was one of the early urban electrified lines. In Europe, the Valtellina line in Italy, opened in 1902, used three-phase alternating current, and the Swiss and Italian railways developed electrification in the mountains, where the hydroelectric power available made electric traction attractive. The Mount Cenis, Gotthard, and Simplon lines were electrified in the early twentieth century, and electric traction became standard on many mountain routes.

The development of alternating current was crucial. Direct-current systems required substations at short intervals and were expensive to extend across long distances, but alternating current could be transformed to high voltages for transmission and reduced to a lower voltage for the locomotive. The French railways adopted 25 kilovolt, 50 hertz alternating current for their main lines after the Second World War, and this system became the standard for much of the world's electrified railway. The German railways used 15 kilovolt, 16⅔ hertz alternating current, a system inherited from the early German electrification experiments. Britain's main-line electrification used 25 kilovolt alternating current on the West Coast Main Line from the 1960s and direct current on the Southern Region and other lines.

Diesel traction offered another alternative. The diesel engine, invented in the 1890s by Rudolf Diesel, was efficient and could run on oil rather than coal. Early diesel locomotives appeared in the 1910s and 1920s, but they were initially limited by the reliability of the engines and the difficulty of transmitting power from engine to wheels. The diesel-electric locomotive, in which the diesel engine drove a generator that supplied electric motors on the axles, solved the transmission problem and became the dominant form of diesel traction. The General Motors Electro-Motive Division, later EMD, built diesel-electric locomotives that became standard across North America, and its streamlined passenger units of the late 1930s demonstrated the speed and reliability of the design. Diesel traction spread rapidly after the Second World War, replacing steam on many lines because it required less maintenance, offered better availability, and did not require the labour-intensive servicing of coal and water.

## Decline, Reform, and the Politics of the Railway

The middle years of the twentieth century were difficult for many railways. Road transport and the private automobile offered a flexible and increasingly attractive alternative for passengers and freight, and air travel took many long-distance passengers away from trains. In the United States, the growth of the interstate highway system and the expansion of commercial aviation caused a steep decline in railway passenger traffic, and many passenger services were withdrawn. Freight traffic also shifted to trucks for much of the goods movement that had once been the railway's core business. The companies that had built the great networks of the nineteenth century struggled to adjust, and several of them went into bankruptcy. The Penn Central, formed by the merger of the Pennsylvania and New York Central railroads, collapsed in 1970, and its failure led to the creation of Conrail and, later, the national passenger operator Amtrak.

In Britain, the railways were grouped into four large companies in 1923 under the Railways Act of 1921, a reform intended to bring stability to an industry that had been weakened by the First World War. The four companies, the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, the London and North Eastern Railway, the Great Western Railway, and the Southern Railway, continued to operate until nationalisation in 1948, when the railways were brought into public ownership as British Railways. The nationalised network was modernised in the 1950s and 1960s, with the introduction of diesel and electric traction and the development of new rolling stock. But the network was also subject to heavy losses, and the passenger services on many branch and rural lines were uneconomic. The Beeching Report of 1963, written by Richard Beeching, recommended the closure of a large number of lines and stations, and the subsequent withdrawal of services transformed the rail map of Britain. Many communities lost their railway links, and the debate about the wisdom of those closures continues.

The railways of continental Europe followed a different path. The French and German railways were generally state-owned or heavily state-supported, and they were kept in service through periods when the British and American networks were contracting. The French railways, the Société Nationale des Chemins de fer Français, were created in 1938 by the merger of the principal companies, and they were later the basis of the successful modernisation of the French network. The German railways, the Deutsche Bundesbahn in the west and the Deutsche Reichsbahn in the east, were divided after the Second World War and reunified in 1994 as the Deutsche Bahn. The state role in European railways has generally been stronger than in the United States, and this has shaped the approach to investment, planning, and regulation.

The European Union has since played a growing role in railway policy. Directives on the separation of infrastructure and operations, on access for competing operators, and on interoperability have sought to create a single railway market across the continent. Britain's railways were privatised in the 1990s under the Railways Act of 1993, with the track owned by Railtrack, later replaced by Network Rail, and passenger services run by franchised private train operating companies. The privatisation was controversial, and the subsequent accidents, cost overruns, and service problems led to a reorganisation of the system in the 2020s. Japan's railways were privatised in 1987, when the national railway was divided into regional companies, and the Japanese network has since been regarded as one of the most efficient in the world. The United States and the United Kingdom have often been contrasted with the European and Japanese models, and the debate about the proper balance between public ownership, private operation, and competitive access continues.

Freight railways have also gone through significant changes. In the United States, deregulation under the Staggers Rail Act of 1980 allowed the railroads to set their own rates and to abandon unprofitable lines. The freight network was consolidated into a small number of large companies, which invested heavily in more efficient operations, including longer trains, double-stacked container cars, and the use of computerised scheduling. The result was a revival of American freight railways, which became more profitable and more competitive with trucks for long-distance haulage. In Europe, freight railways have struggled to compete with road haulage, though they remain important for bulk commodities and for certain international flows.

## High-Speed Rail and the Modern Network

The development of high-speed rail changed the relationship between railways and their passengers. The idea that trains could run at speeds well above the normal limits of conventional railways was not new. The 1930s had seen speed records, and the experiments of the postwar years had shown that steel wheels on steel rails could support much higher speeds than most railways used. Yet the practical demands of high speed were considerable. Tracks had to be straightened and levelled, curves had to be eased, signalling had to be upgraded, and trains had to be designed to run safely at high speeds with a stable ride. The first true high-speed railway was built in Japan, and its success shaped the high-speed programmes of other countries.

The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, the so-called bullet train, opened on 1 October 1964, a few days before the Tokyo Olympic Games. The line linked Tokyo with Osaka, a distance of around 515 kilometres, and it was built to a standard gauge with a new alignment designed for high speed. The trains, known as the 0 Series, ran at up to 210 kilometres per hour, and they transformed travel between Japan's two largest cities. The Shinkansen was an extraordinary engineering achievement, and it showed that high-speed rail could carry large numbers of passengers at high frequency with an excellent safety record. The line was built with high-quality track, automatic train control, and a dedicated right of way that separated it from other traffic. The Shinkansen's safety record, with no passenger fatalities from derailment or collision in its early decades, became a benchmark for the rest of the world.

France followed with the TGV, the Train à Grande Vitesse. The first TGV line, from Paris to Lyon, opened in 1981 and reduced the journey time between the two cities substantially. The TGV was a more radical departure from conventional railways than the Shinkansen, because it used articulated trainsets, in which the carriages shared bogies and were permanently coupled, and because it was designed from the start to run at high speed on dedicated lines. tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.
